items.text: Self-attention lets every token weigh every other token in the sequence, so the model can link a pronoun to a noun many words earlier in a single step.
Attention computes softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)) V: queries are matched against keys, and the resulting weights mix the values. The sqrt(d) scaling keeps the softmax from saturating.
Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel, so different heads can track different relationships, like syntax in one head and coreference in another.
Decoder-only models use causal masking: each token can attend only to earlier positions, which is what makes left-to-right next-token prediction possible.
Standard self-attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length because every token attends to every other. Doubling the context roughly quadruples attention compute.
Transformers have no built-in sense of order. Positional encodings, such as rotary embeddings (RoPE), inject position so 'dog bites man' differs from 'man bites dog'.
An LLM is trained on next-token prediction: given the text so far, it outputs a probability distribution over its vocabulary for the next token.
Encoder-only models (bidirectional) suit classification and embeddings, decoder-only models suit open-ended generation, and encoder-decoder models suit translation.
FlashAttention computes exact attention in tiles that fit in fast on-chip memory, cutting slow memory traffic. Same math, much faster, far less memory.
Models read tokens, not characters or words. A token is often a word fragment; in English one token averages roughly four characters, or about three-quarters of a word.
Byte-pair encoding builds a vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent symbol pairs, so common words become one token and rare words split into pieces.
Tokenization is why models struggle to count letters: they see 'strawberry' as a few multi-letter chunks, not as individual characters.
Non-English text and code often need more tokens per word than English prose, which means higher cost and less usable context for the same content.
Count tokens with the target model's own tokenizer. Model families tokenize the same text differently, so text that fits one limit may overflow another.
An embedding maps text to a dense vector so that similar meanings land close together. 'car' and 'automobile' end up near each other despite sharing no letters.
Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors and ignores their length. For unit-normalized vectors it produces the same ranking as the dot product.
Vectors from different embedding models live in different spaces and cannot be compared. Switching models means re-embedding the whole corpus.
Bi-encoders embed query and document separately, so documents can be precomputed. Cross-encoders read both together: more accurate, but too slow to run over a whole corpus.
Embedding similarity captures topical relatedness, not truth or negation. 'X is safe' and 'X is not safe' can produce very similar vectors.
Some embedding models are trained so vectors can be truncated to fewer dimensions (Matryoshka embeddings), trading a little accuracy for cheaper storage and search.
Semantic search often misses exact identifiers like error codes, SKUs or function names. Keyword search handles those well, so combine the two.
The context window is the total token budget for one call: system prompt, history, retrieved documents, tool definitions and the generated output all share it.
Lost in the middle: models tend to use information at the start and end of a long context more reliably than facts buried in the middle.
A big context window is not free. Every extra token adds latency and cost, and irrelevant text can distract the model and lower answer quality.
With long documents, put the material first and the question or instruction at the end; many models answer more accurately with that ordering.
Temperature divides the logits before softmax. Low values sharpen the distribution toward the top token; high values flatten it for more varied, riskier output.
Temperature 0 approximates greedy decoding, but outputs can still differ between runs because of server-side batching and floating-point nondeterminism.
Top-k sampling keeps only the k most likely tokens before sampling. It trims the long tail of nonsense but ignores how confident the model actually is.
Top-p (nucleus) sampling keeps the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities sum to p, so the candidate pool shrinks when the model is confident and grows when it is not.
Use low temperature for extraction, classification and code, where consistency matters; use higher temperature for brainstorming and creative variety.
Logprobs expose the probability the model assigned to each output token. Useful as a confidence signal, but they are not calibrated probabilities of being correct.
Pretraining teaches language and world knowledge by predicting the next token over massive text. The result is a powerful autocompleter, not yet a helpful assistant.
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) trains a pretrained model on curated prompt-response pairs, teaching it to follow instructions and use a consistent format.
RLHF: humans rank pairs of responses, a reward model learns those preferences, and the LLM is then optimized with reinforcement learning to score highly on it.
RLAIF replaces human preference labels with judgments from an AI model, often guided by a written set of principles, so feedback can scale cheaply.
DPO trains directly on preference pairs (chosen vs rejected) with a simple classification-style loss, skipping the separate reward model and RL loop of RLHF.
Reward hacking: optimizing against a learned reward model can find outputs that score high without being better, such as longer or more flattering answers.
Fine-tuning is best for teaching format, style or narrow behavior. For fresh or frequently changing facts, retrieval is usually more reliable and easier to update.
Catastrophic forgetting: fine-tuning hard on a narrow dataset can erode abilities the model had before. Mix in general data or use lighter-weight methods.
Try prompting first, then retrieval, then fine-tuning. Each step costs more to build and maintain, so move up only when evals show you need to.
A few thousand clean, consistent fine-tuning examples usually beat a much larger noisy set. The model learns your mistakes as faithfully as your good examples.

LoRA, the most common PEFT (parameter-efficient fine-tuning) method, freezes the base weights and learns a small low-rank update, two thin matrices per adapted layer, so only a tiny fraction of parameters is trained.
LoRA adapters are small files. You can keep one base model loaded and swap adapters per task or per customer instead of hosting many full models.
A trained LoRA update can be merged into the base weights, so the fine-tuned model runs with zero extra inference latency.
QLoRA trains LoRA adapters on top of a base model quantized to 4 bits, making fine-tuning of large models feasible on a single GPU.
LoRA rank sets adapter capacity. Low ranks often suffice for style or format changes; bigger domain shifts may need a higher rank or more adapted layers.
Quantization stores weights in fewer bits, such as 8 or 4 instead of 16, cutting memory use and often speeding inference at a small accuracy cost.
Token-by-token generation is usually limited by memory bandwidth, not math, so smaller quantized weights that load faster often speed up decoding directly.
A few outlier values in activations make naive quantization lossy. Methods that rescale channels or keep outliers in higher precision preserve quality at low bit widths.
Memory rule of thumb: parameters times bytes per weight. A 7B-parameter model needs about 14 GB at 16-bit and about 3.5 GB at 4-bit, before KV cache and overhead.
Distillation trains a small student model to imitate a larger teacher, keeping much of the teacher's skill at a fraction of the inference cost.
Soft targets carry more signal than hard labels: the teacher's full probability distribution tells the student which wrong answers are almost right.
A practical distillation recipe: have a strong model produce high-quality outputs for your task, then fine-tune a small model on them and evaluate on real traffic.
Mixture of experts replaces one feed-forward block with many expert blocks plus a router that sends each token to only a few of them.
MoE decouples total parameters from compute per token: the model can hold many experts, but each token pays only for the few it is routed to.
MoE models still need memory for every expert even though each token uses only a few, so they are cheap in compute per token but heavy in memory.
KV cache: generation stores the keys and values of every previous token, so each new token computes attention against the cache instead of reprocessing the prefix.
KV cache memory grows linearly with sequence length and batch size. At long contexts it can rival or exceed the memory taken by the model weights.
Generation has two phases: prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel and is compute bound; decode emits one token at a time and is memory bound.
Time to first token is dominated by prompt prefill; the token rate after that is dominated by decode. Optimize whichever one your users actually feel.
Speculative decoding: a small draft model proposes several tokens, and the large model verifies them all in one parallel pass, keeping the longest accepted prefix.
With proper acceptance rules, speculative decoding yields exactly the large model's output distribution. It is a pure speed-up, not an approximation.
Few-shot prompting: include a handful of input-output examples. The model copies their format and style, so make the examples diverse and correct.
Examples are strong signals. If every few-shot example has a short answer or the same label, the model will over-produce that pattern.
Chain-of-thought: asking the model to reason step by step before answering improves multi-step math and logic by giving it tokens to think with.
Put the final answer after the reasoning, not before. An answer written first cannot benefit from reasoning that comes after it.
Structured output: supply a JSON schema and use the provider's schema or constrained mode where available, instead of hoping free text will parse.
Constrained decoding masks invalid tokens at each step so the output always matches a grammar or schema. It guarantees valid syntax, not correct content.
System prompts set the persistent role, rules and tone for a conversation. Keep them focused; a pile of conflicting rules degrades compliance with all of them.
Delimiters like XML tags or triple quotes separate instructions from data, so the model can tell which text to follow and which text to process.
Say what to do, not just what to avoid. 'Answer in plain flowing prose' works better than 'Do not use markdown'.
Explain why a rule exists. 'Keep it short, this is read aloud on a phone' helps the model generalize better than a bare 'be brief'.
Give the model an out: explicitly allow 'I don't know' or 'not in the document' to reduce invented answers when the information is missing.
Prefilling the start of the assistant's reply, such as an opening brace, strongly steers the output format on APIs that support it.
RAG retrieves relevant documents at query time and places them in the prompt, grounding answers in your own data without retraining the model.
Chunking: split documents into passages small enough to be specific but large enough to stand alone. Split on headings or paragraphs, not mid-sentence.
Chunk overlap repeats a little text across chunk boundaries so a fact that straddles two chunks can still be retrieved intact.
Contextual chunking prepends a short description of the source document to each chunk, so 'revenue grew 3%' still says which company and which year.
BM25 ranks documents by keyword matches, weighting rare terms more and saturating repeated ones. It is fast, needs no training and excels at exact terms.
Hybrid search runs BM25 and dense vector search side by side and fuses the results, catching both exact keywords and paraphrased meaning.
Reciprocal rank fusion merges ranked lists by summing 1/(k + rank) for each document, so it combines retrievers without calibrating their scores.
Reranking: retrieve a broad candidate set cheaply, then rescore the top results with a cross-encoder so the truly relevant passages come first.
Metadata filters on date, product, language or permissions narrow retrieval to the right slice, preventing semantically similar but wrong results.
Enforce access control at retrieval time. If a user may not see a document, it must never reach the prompt, because the model may quote it.
Citation grounding: have the model cite a chunk ID for each claim, then check that the cited text actually supports the claim before showing it.
Evaluate retrieval separately from generation. If the right chunk never reaches the top results, no amount of prompt tuning can fix the answer.
HyDE: have the model write a hypothetical answer, embed it, and search with that vector. Answers often resemble the target documents more than questions do.
Exact nearest-neighbor search compares a query to every vector. Approximate indexes trade a little recall for search that is orders of magnitude faster.
HNSW builds a layered graph of vectors: search starts on sparse upper layers for long hops, then descends to denser layers to refine the nearest neighbors.
HNSW tuning: higher M and efConstruction build a better graph at more memory and build time; higher efSearch raises recall at more query time.
IVF clusters vectors around centroids and searches only the few clusters nearest the query. The nprobe setting trades recall for speed.
Filtered vector search is tricky: filtering after the approximate search can leave too few results. Check how your database combines filters with the index.
A golden set is a curated collection of inputs with known good outputs or grading criteria. It is the foundation for every LLM quality decision.
Build golden sets from real user traffic and past failures, not only invented examples. Include edge cases, adversarial inputs and tricky negatives.
LLM-as-judge pitfalls: judges tend to favor longer answers, whichever option comes first, and outputs from their own model family. Randomize order and spot-check.
Give an LLM judge a specific rubric and ask for its reasoning before the verdict. Clear pass/fail criteria are more reliable than 1-to-10 scores.
Calibrate an LLM judge by measuring its agreement with human labels on a sample before trusting it to grade at scale.
Regression testing: rerun the eval suite on every prompt, model or retrieval change. A fix for one case often silently breaks another.
Benchmark contamination: if test questions leaked into training data, scores overstate real ability. Private, task-specific evals are more trustworthy.
Read the outputs. Aggregate scores hide failure patterns that become obvious after reviewing a few dozen real responses by hand.
Hallucinations happen because models generate plausible continuations, not verified facts. Fluency and confident tone are not evidence of accuracy.
Ask the model to extract verbatim quotes from the sources before answering, then answer only from those quotes. Claims with no supporting quote get dropped.
Models are especially prone to fabricating specifics: citations, URLs, quotes, statistics and API names. Verify these mechanically, not by eye.
Consistency check: ask the same question several times at nonzero temperature. Facts that change between samples are less likely to be true.
Offload what models do poorly: use a calculator for math, search for current events and a database for exact records instead of trusting recall.
Knowledge cutoff: a model knows nothing that happened after its training data was collected. Supply recent facts in the context.
Prompt caching reuses the already-processed prefix of a prompt across calls, cutting cost and time to first token for repeated instructions or documents.
Prompt caches match exact prefixes. Put stable content first (instructions, tools, documents) and variable content last, or every call misses the cache.
A timestamp or request ID near the top of a prompt silently defeats prompt caching, because everything after the first changed token must be recomputed.
Output tokens usually cost more and take longer than input tokens because they are generated one at a time. Asking for concise output saves both.
Streaming does not make generation faster, but showing tokens as they arrive greatly improves perceived latency for users.
Batch APIs trade latency for lower cost. Use them for offline jobs like evals, backfills and bulk classification that nobody is waiting on.
Measure cost per successful task, not per call. A cheap model that needs three retries can cost more than a stronger one that succeeds once.
Semantic caching returns a stored answer for queries similar to past ones. Great for repetitive FAQs, risky when a small wording change alters the meaning.
Prompt injection: text the model processes contains instructions that override yours. Direct injection comes from the user; indirect injection hides in content the model reads.
In RAG, one poisoned document in the index can inject instructions into every answer that retrieves it. Treat indexed content as untrusted input.
Jailbreaks use role-play, hypotheticals, unusual encodings or long multi-turn pressure to push a model past its safety training.
Defend against jailbreaks in layers: model safety training plus input and output classifiers, rate limits and monitoring. No single layer is enough.
Anything in the prompt, including the system prompt, can potentially be extracted by a determined user. Never put secrets or keys there.
Redact or pseudonymize PII before sending text to a model or writing it to logs, and restore it afterward only where it is truly needed.
Validate model output before it reaches other systems. Treat generated SQL, HTML or shell commands as untrusted input to prevent downstream injection.
Markdown images in model output can exfiltrate data: an injected instruction can encode secrets into an image URL that the client fetches automatically.
Vision-language models split an image into patches, encode each patch as a vector, and feed those vectors to the language model much like tokens.
Images consume context tokens too, often scaling with resolution. Downscale images to the level of detail the task actually needs.
Vision models can misread small text, miscount objects and misjudge precise positions. Crop and enlarge the region of interest for fine details.
CLIP-style models train image and text encoders together so matching pairs land close in one shared space, enabling text-to-image search and zero-shot labels.
Diffusion models learn to reverse noise: training corrupts images with noise step by step, and the model learns to predict and remove that noise.
Image generation starts from pure random noise and denoises it over many steps, with the text prompt guiding each step toward a matching image.
Latent diffusion denoises in the compressed latent space of an autoencoder rather than raw pixels, making generation far cheaper.
Classifier-free guidance compares predictions with and without the prompt and pushes further toward the prompt. Higher guidance: more literal, less diverse.
